background_notes.fact: For the jointly smooth u and fixed t0>0, g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0) is smooth on R^n and ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u+u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u, with all factors evaluated at (x,t0).

grounds.reason: Joint smoothness gives all derivatives appearing here and their smoothness.
There are finitely many real vector components and a valid spatial coordinate.
Fixes t0,j and defines g from those smooth factors.

background_notes.justification: Expand the Euclidean dot product as the finite sum of products of scalar components. The scalar product rule in coordinate j yields the two displayed sums, and finite sums and products of smooth functions remain smooth. This is a local differentiation step, not an integration-by-parts premise.

background_notes.fact: For fixed remaining coordinates y, the affine insertion line gives (g∘I_j(y,·))'(z)=∂_{x_j}g(I_j(y,z)). This derivative is continuous, hence measurable and bounded on [-R,R], and therefore interval integrable there.

grounds.reason: F001 establishes smoothness of g and its coordinate derivative.
I_j varies only coordinate j, with velocity the jth coordinate unit vector.
The chosen R is a positive finite real.
Defines the line functions and restricts to the compact interval.

background_notes.justification: The chain rule evaluates the differential of g on that unit vector, giving precisely ∂_{x_j}g. Continuous real functions on a compact interval attain a finite bound B and are Borel measurable. The integral of their absolute value is at most B times 2R, which is finite; interval and closed-interval integrals agree because endpoints have Lebesgue measure zero.

background_notes.fact: Let λ be Lebesgue measure on R^(n-1) restricted to [-R,R]^(n-1) and ν Lebesgue measure on R restricted to [-R,R]. The insertion bijection I_j pushes λ×ν to μ restricted to Q=[-R,R]^n. These are finite measures, so they are s-finite. For n=1 the R^0 factor is the singleton with mass one.

grounds.reason: D005 identifies spatial Lebesgue measure with the product of its coordinate Lebesgue measures, also on boxes.
n≥1 makes the remaining coordinate count n-1 nonnegative.
I_j inserts the missing coordinate in the specified order.
Gives the rectangle comparison and the explicit R^0 convention.

background_notes.justification: Insertion and its inverse are coordinate maps, hence Borel measurable. A rectangle in Q has preimage the rectangle of its remaining coordinates times its jth interval. Its measure is the product of the same side lengths as its spatial product measure. These rectangles form a generating intersection-closed family containing Q. Finite-measure uniqueness (the equality class extends from rectangles to their generated sigma algebra by the usual monotone-class argument) gives the stated pushforward identity, and thus equality of integrals under insertion. Coordinate box measures are finite products of finite interval lengths; in zero dimensions the empty product is one. A finite measure is itself a countable sum of finite measures by appending zero measures, giving s-finiteness.

background_notes.fact: The real function v(y,z)=∂_{x_j}g(I_j(y,z)) is integrable for the restricted finite product measure used in A002.

grounds.reason: The domain carrying the measure is the compact product box, with its finite restricted coordinate measures.

background_notes.justification: The continuous insertion map makes v continuous and thus Borel measurable. Its absolute value has a finite bound B on the compact product box. The product measure is concentrated there, so its absolute integral is at most B(2R)^n<∞. This verifies the integrability premise of the supplied Fubini theorem without exchanging any unsupported limit.

background_notes.fact: If real integrable functions a,b on R^n vanish outside C⊂Q, then their integrals, and that of a+b, equal their respective integrals on Q, and ∫(a+b)=∫a+∫b. Here a=∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u and b=u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u at t0.

grounds.reason: F001 supplies both summands, their absolute integrability, their support in C, and their sum ∂_{x_j}g.
F003 gives zero for the box integral of their sum.
C lies inside Q, a measurable coordinate box.

background_notes.justification: Integrability is preserved by addition since |a+b|≤|a|+|b|. Lebesgue integral linearity for integrable functions gives the sum identity. Splitting the integral over the measurable box and its complement adds a zero term because each function vanishes on that complement. Substituting F003 therefore gives 0=∫a+∫b with finite real terms; dot-product symmetry then gives the required rearranged equality.
